title: Raised Clothed in Glory
english: …beauty, and is admired, so in this same way the human body too is sown in corruption, in weakness and in dishonor, but will come back to life clothed in honor and incorruption, and in power as well (1 Corinthians 15:42–43).

The sober watchfulness of the one who speaks for God deserves our admiration. For his faith is firmly grounded, and he is confident that the body will come back to life in every way and without fail; so he likens the body's corruption to sowing, and with great skill and wisdom makes the nature of the thing match the example at every point. So, he says, like the grain, the body will not come back to life bare, but richly clothed with incorruption and glory, and with strength besides, and enriched also with this: that it comes to be of a spiritual mind, since the grace from above and the incomparable power of the Creator of all in a way refashion what is in it into the very opposite.

For corruption and weakness and lack of beauty dwell in the body that has fallen and been sown, as it were, in the earth, and a natural mind as well, which we say is the same as the fleshly and more earthly mind. But it was not so by nature when it was brought into being in the beginning; these things crept in through the transgression and the sentence of death. Since our nature is being called back to what it was in the beginning, the putting off of what came in between is necessarily brought about by the power and working of God, and in exchange there is brought in a share in the good things that were ours first, in the beginning.

For we have been renewed in Christ, as the Scriptures say. A holy prophet said, “Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands grow slack. The Lord your God is in you, mighty to save you, and He will renew you in His love” (Zephaniah 3:16–17). For when God the Father loved us, then, at that very time, He renewed us in Christ. And indeed it is true that all things in Him are “a new creation; the old things have passed away, and new things have come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

What old things does he mean? Those that have gone by. And what new things? Those that have been brought in. The old are corruption, and weakness, and dishonor besides, and the faults of the natural mind; the new, through Christ, are glory and incorruption and power and the spiritual mind. For our body will be spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44).

What would “spiritual” mean, O teacher of the mysteries? Does he mean that it will no longer be flesh, and will in no way be composed, as it is now, of bones and sinews, through which the nature of our body is made complete, but will rather be thin and airy, hardly more solid than a shadow? Not at all. For if some think this is how things stand, then surely it will not be the very thing that falls into the earth that comes back to life, but something else beside it, in no way like the first.

I would say that “spiritual” means not what has the form of a shadow, that is, of a bodiless spirit, but rather what has stood apart from, and indeed been wholly set free from, the fleshly and more earthly mind. “For if there is,” he says, “a natural body, there is also…

title: The Natural Adam and the Life-Giving Christ
english: …a spiritual one” (1 Corinthians 15:44). For suppose someone chooses to call our body from the earth “natural.” One would reasonably not attach to it the form of a soul, but would rather turn the force of the word to the natural, that is, the fleshly, mind, just as we understand our own human wisdom to be “natural” and “earthly” (James 3:15). So too, even if it is called a natural body, one who attaches to it the form of a soul would not, I think, escape the charge of going astray. Otherwise, in what sense are some people, while still alive and still in these very bodies from the earth, called natural and others spiritual? For it is written, “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; but the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:14–15).

Since it followed that he should confirm his argument on this point by facts as well, he adds, “The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). So he called Adam natural; for this, I think, is what being made “a living soul” means: that he was not wholly free from fleshly desires. For the appetites that look and turn toward the passions of the flesh, even if they have the law to speak in their defense, would still in truth be charges against fleshly weakness, if one looks at the nature of what is done.

I mean something like this: “Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). For the Maker of all has planted in the nature of the body a movement of appetite that stirs the living creature to the desire for children. For it was said to man, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28); and, he says, “He who formed them in the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4; Genesis 1:27). So the desire that looks only to having children is blameless; yet as far as the nature of the act goes, the passion would be fleshly, that is, natural. And so it is with the other blameless passions as well.

So the first man Adam became a living soul; but the second, the one from heaven, that is, Christ, became not a soul but rather a life-giving spirit. For God the Word, who came forth from God the Father and is God by nature, united the human to Himself and lived not a human life like ours, but a life divine, fitting for God, and wholly blameless. For “He committed no sin” (1 Peter 2:22): He kept His mind untouched by unseemly pleasures, and it could not be caught by desires for food. For even though He is seen to have taken food and drink, so that He might be believed to be truly a man like us, still He partook of them freely. For He was in the flesh for our sake, in keeping with the plan of salvation, and yet again above the flesh; for He was a life-giving spirit as God.

But our forefather Adam admitted a desire for food that was not wholly free from blame. For he had been made a living soul, and, overcome by the pleasure of food, he ate from the tree of life, although the divine law forbade him to do so (Genesis 2:17; 3:6).

title: The First and the Second Adam
english: That the word “natural,” then, would suggest to us not a difference of nature, but rather a quality of life, of character and of ways, by which one person is held fast by the more earthly and fleshly mind, and another shines out in the freedom of the Spirit, he shows clearly from Adam, the first and the second. For both came to be in earthly bodies; but the quality, so to speak, of the mind, and indeed the choice to live in a different way, showed the one to be natural, and the other to be incomparably better, that is, spiritual.

“But the spiritual is not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual” (1 Corinthians 15:46). In a way he takes hold of the times in which they came to be, and says, “But the spiritual is not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual.” Since he said that the body is sown in the earth natural, he shows plainly that it is not foreign to human nature to pass from a natural mind to a spiritual one, and that the natural would be older than the spiritual. And what proof could there be of such things? “The first man was from the earth, made of dust,” and so on (1 Corinthians 15:47).

The first man, he says, that is, Adam, had been made a living soul, that is, earthly and fleshly; but the second is from heaven. For even though the Word of God became flesh, as the Scriptures say (John 1:14), yet He was [lacuna] also the One from heaven and “above all,” in the words of John (John 3:31). So both, as I said, were in earthly bodies, but they were not also equal in disposition, that is, in their way of life. For the first was of a fleshly mind, while the second, the One from heaven, was a life-giving spirit.

“And just as we have borne the image of the man of dust,” that is, the likeness to Adam, being overcome by passions and weak toward sins, and brought besides under the yokes of corruption, “so let us also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49), that is, of Christ: becoming superior to love of the flesh and to any wish to go on sinning, and having already conquered death itself, which of old was terrible and hard to face and ruled savagely over us as a tyrant.

“Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). By this too he establishes the mystery of the resurrection. For as long as the human body is flesh and blood, that is, mortal and corruptible, it could not inherit the kingdom of God, that is, unending existence. So it is wholly necessary that corruption be swallowed up and what readily withers be done away, and that the body itself be refashioned into incorruption and made radiant with a divine and unspeakable glory; for then it will inherit the kingdom of God.

“Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51). Great and truly heavenly is the mystery, and it was surely revealed to him through Christ who spoke in him (2 Corinthians 13:3), “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).
